headline: Arini losses deepen to 26% as European junk bond selloff accelerates
snippet: Arini Capital Management's flagship hedge fund has lost approximately 26% this year as a selloff in Europe's riskiest corporate debt forces the $21.7bn credit manager to adopt a more defensive investment approach, according to a report by Bloomberg. The fund, which managed $7.5bn at the end of July, is on course for its first annual loss since founder Hamza Lemssouguer launched the strategy in 2022. Lemssouguer, a former Credit Suisse credit trader, has reportedly reduced new purchases to focus on managing existing positions, withdrawing a significant source of liquidity from Europe's distressed debt market. The retreat comes as European triple-C rated corporate bonds face their longest losing streak since 2018, with October potentially marking their worst monthly performance in four years. Rising interest rates, higher energy prices and concerns over corporate creditworthiness have intensified pressure on heavily indebted borrowers, while other credit hedge funds have also suffered losses. Sona Asset Management's flagship fund declined 3.1% in the first half of October, putting it on course for its worst month since launching in 2016. Arini's concentrated exposure to distressed borrowers has contributed to the drawdown, including positions in Aston Martin and Altice International. Aston Martin's bonds fell from approximately 55 cents on the dollar at the beginning of October to 47 cents by Wednesday, while debt issued by Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection has dropped below 75 cents from more than 92 cents at the end of September. Some investors have reportedly become reluctant to purchase securities in which Arini holds sizeable positions. Despite the losses, Arini continues to attract capital, having raised $1.5bn for its credit strategy and reopened the fund to existing investors. More than $400m of the new commitments was allocated at the beginning of October, with the remainder scheduled for deployment through February. The downturn marks a sharp reversal for a manager whose flagship fund returned 25.8% in 2023, 20.8% in 2024 and 8.6% in 2025. However, some credit investors believe the market dislocation could create opportunities to acquire distressed securities at attractive valuations, even as concerns grow over further losses across Europe's lowest-rated debt markets.

headline: Cozy Magical Sim Witchbrook Gets A January Release Date
snippet: Witchbrook is a game I've been looking forward to for a while, and today's Nintendo Indie World showcase finally confirmed the game's release date: January 28. Any game from Chucklefish, best known for publishing Stardew Valley and developing the Wargroove series, is worthy of my attention, and Witchbrook looks more exciting the more we see of it. See it for yourself in the release date trailer below. The game mixes cute pixel art with a robust suite of magical gameplay systems. As you go to a witch college to learn spells, you'll also build a life in the town, making friends, working jobs, decorating your home, and more. It was an appealing pitch when it was announced nearly 10 years ago in 2017, and it remains so to this day. After a long stretch of relative silence, last year the game was scheduled to launch sometime in 2026. Obviously, the team has faced some delays since then, but we're just glad it's actually coming out. headline: Sudan: More than half of children assessed in Jebel Marra stunted as drought worsens hunger crisis
snippet: KHARTOUM, 28 October 2026 – More than half of children assessed in Jebel Marra, one of Sudan's most isolated and food-insecure regions, are chronically malnourished, according to new Save the Children data, highlighting the growing impact of conflict and the El-Niño weather event. New data from Save the Children in Central Jebal Marra found 57% of children are chronically malnourished (known as stunted) while 15% of children assessed – or nearly one in six - were acutely malnourished [1]. Stunting, meaning a child has low height for their age, reflects chronic or recurrent undernutrition while acute malnutrition or wasting, meaning a child has low weight for their height due to recent or ongoing severe weight loss or failure to gain weight. Both forms of malnutrition can have lasting consequences for children's health and development. As a result of conflict, food shortages, limited access to healthcare, clean water and sanitation, the survey found that over four in 10 (43%) children in Central Jebel Marra had been ill in the two weeks preceding the survey. A total of 69% of households surveyed relied on unsafe or untreated water. The findings underline the urgent need for an integrated response to malnutrition that addresses not only children's immediate nutritional needs, but also access to food, healthcare, safe water, sanitation and protection from diseases, said Save the Children. Jebel Marra, a usually fertile and food producing area of Sudan, is being hit by the combined effects of conflict, severe drought, disrupted livelihoods and a critically underfunded humanitarian response. Lack of rainfall has also led to shortages of animal fodder, placing further pressure on herders. Global hunger monitor, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), last week warned that conflict, displacement and severe El Niño-induced drought are increasing the risk of famine in parts of Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan. The ongoing conflict in Sudan has caused the world’s largest displacement crisis, forcing about 11 million people from their homes, with at least 19 million people – or two in every five Sudanese – facing acute food insecurity, according to the World Food Programme. The impact of drought and Sudan’s wider hunger crisis is also being felt beyond Darfur. In Gedaref, seven-month-old Hamza* lost his mother shortly after birth and was cared for by his grandmother, Khadija*. When he became seriously ill, she took him to a Save the Children-supported stabilisation centre, where he was diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition and received treatment. He is now recovering. “When we arrived at the stabilisation centre, the doctors and nurses immediately began treating him,” said Khadija. “Today, he smiles, plays and looks like a different child.” Claire Henery, Country Director for Save the Children in Sudan, said: “Children in Sudan are being hit by crisis upon crisis. Conflict has already devastated livelihoods and access to essential services, and drought is deepening an already severe crisis. “ Our latest findings from Central Jebel Marra show children facing both acute malnutrition and the long-term effects of inadequate nutrition. At the same time, many families lack safe water, and children remain vulnerable to disease. “The international community cannot look away. We urgently need a large-scale integrated response and sustained access to provide food security, life-saving nutrition, healthcare and clean water while strengthening the systems children depend on.” Save the Children has worked in Sudan since 1983 and provides programming for children and families affected by conflict, displacement, extreme poverty and hunger. Save the Children has recently launched a $300 million global humanitarian nutrition initiative for 2026–2028 bringing together public and private funders to treat and prevent child malnutrition and illness in the toughest humanitarian contexts – including in Sudan. Partners joining this initiative are helping reshape the future of humanitarian nutrition, redesigning the way the world treats malnutrition – from a reactive system focused on treating crisis to one that prevents it.
